Short version: for N1 itself, the endpoint ambiguity you've spotted is not a problem, and you can record it as such. What the protocol needs from N1 is narrower than "pin down `g_ω` completely."

**What N1 actually has to settle.** The load-bearing fact is that `g_ω` vanishes identically for `x > 1` and the cutoff sits at exactly `1`, not at some other `c`. That is what makes `κ_ω(t) = e^{−t/2} g_ω(e^{−t}) 1_{t>0}` causal with its edge at `t = 0`, and it is what would move the `log 2` threshold if it were wrong. The single point `x = 1` has measure zero, so whether `g_ω(1)` is defined, undefined, or set to either one-sided value changes nothing about `κ_ω` as an `L^1`/`L^2` object and nothing downstream. Transcribe it as printed — "formula on `0<x<1`, zero for `x>1`, value at `1` not specified" — and note that the open/closed question is moot for the same reason. That closes N1.

**Where to look harder, because it feeds later items.** Two regions of `x`, over the range of `ω` the preprint actually uses, which is real `ω ∈ (0, ½]` (that's a regenerable fact from Part 1, so no contamination in telling you). Your remark about `ω > 1` is outside the range that matters, so don't spend effort there.

1. `x → 1^−`. Record what the paper says the one-sided limit is and how it depends on `ω` — in particular whether `g_ω` goes to zero at the edge or has a nonzero limit, and whether any regularity statement is on `(0,1)` only or on all of `(0,∞)`. A nonzero limit means `κ_ω` has a jump at `t = 0`; that feeds the smoothness of the kernel in the Hankel operator (N3) and the "why is the boundary case measure-zero rather than merely small" step in Part 3.

2. `x → 0^+`. Record the stated growth or decay rate of `g_ω` near zero. This is the input for the Mellin-domain fingerprint: the convergence half-plane of `∫_0^1 g_ω(x) x^s dx/x` is determined entirely by the behavior at `0^+` once you know the support ends at `1`. Write that half-plane down from the transcribed rate before reading `§3.1` of either document — that check is still clean and is the one you most want to keep blind.

**One caution on the `L^1`/`L^2` remark.** Don't resolve it as "presumably locally integrable." Transcribe the exact space and domain as printed (`L^1(0,∞)`, `L^1(0,1)`, `L^1_{loc}`, whatever it is), because the Hankel operator in N3 needs a global statement, not a local one, and "presumably" is where a testimony-tier check quietly stops being one. If the paper is ambiguous, the ambiguity is the record; if it later conflicts with what the preprint assumes, that mismatch is a finding, same rule as the domain safeguard in the handoff.

I've deliberately not said anything about what Suzuki's paper contains on any of these points.

parts:
That's a clean transcription, and it has real consequences. Record it exactly as you wrote it, then note the following — all of this is inference from your transcription, not from anything I know about the paper.

**What the three thresholds together tell you.** Continuity above `ω = 1`, `L^2` above `ω = ½`, `L^1` above `ω = 0` is the signature of a power singularity of exponent `ω − 1` at `x = 1^−` (the `L^2` threshold is where `2(ω−1) = −1`, and at `ω = ½` exactly the square is log-divergent, which is why the statement is strict). You can check that reading against the formula on `(0,1)` yourself; it's regenerable.

**Why it matters for this project.** The preprint's range is `ω ∈ (0, ½]`. Across that entire range, by your transcription, `g_ω` is unbounded and not `L^2` near `x = 1`. Translated: `κ_ω(t) = e^{−t/2} g_ω(e^{−t})` has an integrable but non-square-integrable singularity at `t = 0^+`, right at the causal edge, and the layer formula then puts a copy of that singularity at every delay `log n`, including `t = 0` for `n = 1`, which sits in the interior of the sum-coordinate range `(−L, L)` for every `L > 0`. So the kernel of the quadratic form is unbounded at the center of the window for every `ω` the paper uses.

That gives you three concrete things to check against the preprint when you get to Part 3, and I'd add them to the checklist:

1. Does the preprint anywhere assert or silently use that `g_ω`, `κ_ω`, `h_ω`, or `k_ω` is bounded, continuous, or `L^2` for `ω ∈ (0, ½]`? Any such statement is a mismatch with your transcription and is a finding.
2. Does the Hankel operator setup (N3) need `h_ω ∈ L^2` in some sense, and if so how does the preprint get it at `ω ≤ ½`?
3. How do the certificates (the `computer`-status statements S14/S18) handle an unbounded kernel at `t = 0` and at `t = log n`? Interval arithmetic on a function with an integrable singularity inside the window is a different task from interval arithmetic on a continuous one, and this is the load-bearing part of the paper.

**Two smaller points.** Pin down what "locally" scopes over in the `L^1` statement — near `1` only, or on `(0,∞)` — since the global `L^1` property is what the Hankel operator wants. And you still owe yourself the `x → 0^+` rate for the Mellin fingerprint; nothing you've transcribed yet touches that end.

Good — this one is the load-bearing item, and your transcription lines up with the N2 claim as the protocol states it on all three axes that determine where the `n = 2` layer lands: prefactor `1/x` (not `1/√x`), argument `g_ω(n/x)` (not `x/n`), summation over `n ≤ x` (the floor is the same thing). Vanishing on `(0,1)` also matches. Record it as a match and move on; nothing to escalate here.

A few observations, again all inference from what you've transcribed:

**Don't read a definition into the support statement.** "Support in `[1,∞)`" is the closure of the set where the function is nonzero; it says nothing about a value at `x = 1`, and it's the standard way to write it when the function is zero to the left. Your right-limit reading is an over-interpretation, and it doesn't matter anyway — same measure-zero point as N1. Transcribe "value at `1` unspecified; support stated as `[1,∞)`" and leave it.

**The singularity structure is now fully determined, and it's a consistency check you can run.** Since `n ≤ x` forces `n/x ∈ (0,1]`, the only way `g_ω`'s singular point is reached is when `x` is just above an integer `n`, where the `n`-th term has `n/x → 1^−`. So `h_ω` inherits an integrable, non-`L^2` (for `ω ≤ ½`) singularity at every integer from the right, and is regular in between. That is exactly what the "locally `L^1` for `ω > 0`, `L^2` for `ω > ½`" line should say if it's inherited from N1, and it is — so N1 and N2 are mutually consistent on regularity. Worth writing down as a check passed.

**For Part 3.** When you get to substituting this into `k_ω(t) = e^{t/2} h_ω(e^t)`, those right-sided integer singularities become right-sided singularities at `t = log n`, and the `n`-th one switches on precisely at its delay. You should see that structure fall out of the derivation on its own; if what you derive puts the singularity anywhere else, something in the substitution is off. I'll stop there so as not to pre-empt the blind derivation.

**Carry forward.** The `L^2`-fails-for-`ω ≤ ½` fact now stands on two independent statements in [1], which strengthens the three checks I listed last message, especially whether the Hankel setup in N3 or the certificates need square-integrability near `t = 0` and `t = log n`.
